_readme: Chucky's fact nuggets. Edit this file to change what Chucky says - then just reload the game (no rebuild needed).
intro: shown one after another when you start your first game (and from the menu: Chucky's tips).
facts: shown as you play, one at a time, each only once per device (Settings > Hear all the facts again resets that).
Every entry needs a unique "id" and a "text". A fact's optional "when" says what you must have reached first:
logs = logs collected, trees = trees felled, score = points, day = day number, built = structures you built,
throws = logs thrown, chased = wolves/bears/piranhas chased off, swim = times you've gone into the water,
night = nights seen, bitten = piranha bites.
Several keys = all of them. Facts without "when" come up one by one every few minutes of play.
Facts are shown in the order they appear here, at most one every 40 seconds.

intro.text: By the way, I'm a beaver! Woodchucks don't actually "chuck wood" LOL! My first fact nugget for you!
Move me with the joystick (or WASD). In the behind-me camera, left and right turn me and up walks forward. Tap 📷 to switch cameras and slide the zoom on the right.
To chomp a tree, just walk into its trunk and I'll get gnawing. Felled trees drop logs - walk over them to collect them.
Grab logs quickly to build a combo: every 2 logs adds to the multiplier, up to 4x!
Tap 🏗️ to build. Structures in the river count as real dams and score the most points.
In the river, hold 🤿 to dive for sunken logs and fruit. Keep an eye on my breath bar!
Apples and berries heal me. Three berries give me the Zoomies - a burst of speed!
Beware the night: wolves and bears come out. Hold 🪵 and let go to chuck a log at them - a quick tap is a short toss, hold longer for a long lob.

facts.text: Fact nugget: beaver teeth are orange! The enamel has iron in it, which makes it extra tough - and our front teeth never stop growing, so we have to keep gnawing.
Our lips close behind our front teeth, so we can gnaw underwater without getting a mouthful of river.
Myth buster: beavers don't eat fish! We're vegetarians - we munch bark, twigs, leaves and water plants.
Beavers can stay underwater for up to about 15 minutes on one breath. You'll have to settle for a lot less here!
We have see-through eyelids that work like swimming goggles, and our ears and nose close up when we dive.
So what IS a woodchuck? It's another name for a groundhog - a kind of marmot, which is a big ground squirrel. They dig burrows and eat plants. No wood chucking at all!
Beavers are mostly night owls - we do most of our work from dusk until dawn.
Okay, confession: real beavers can't throw logs. That part is pure Chucky magic!
Myth buster: we don't use our tails as trowels to pat down mud. A beaver tail is a rudder, a prop to lean on, a fat store - and a loud alarm when we slap it on the water!
Myth buster: beavers don't live in their dams! We live in lodges or bank burrows. The dam makes a deep pond so our front door can stay underwater, safe from predators.
We can't really choose where a tree falls - sometimes it drops the wrong way or gets hung up in another tree. Watch out!
The sound of running water makes beavers want to build. Scientists found beavers will pile sticks over a speaker playing water sounds!
Beavers are the second-biggest rodents in the world. Only the capybara of South America is bigger.
We have a split 'grooming claw' on our back feet that works like a comb, spreading oil through our fur to keep it waterproof.
Beaver ponds make wetlands that slow floods, clean the water and give homes to fish, frogs, birds and insects. That's why we're called ecosystem engineers.
Myth buster: your vanilla ice cream almost certainly isn't flavoured by beavers. Castoreum, from beaver scent glands, was once used in some flavourings, but today it's very rare in food.
Baby beavers are called kits. They live with their parents and older brothers and sisters in a family colony.
The biggest known beaver dam is in Wood Buffalo National Park in Canada. It's about 850 metres long!
There are two kinds of beaver: the North American beaver and the Eurasian beaver. They look alike, but they can't have babies together.

Ouch! Myth buster: real piranhas rarely attack big animals, and the 'skeleton in seconds' stories are mostly movie magic. They live in South America, not in beaver rivers - this one is a game monster!
Before winter, beavers stash branches underwater next to the lodge - a food pantry they can reach even when the pond freezes over.
Long ago, a giant beaver about the size of a black bear lived in North America. Imagine the size of its dams!
